events.c: Forecasts warned of snowstorms and cloud; the crew had been briefed to avoid the central route.
Five crew members and six passengers departed for Santiago, planning to fly via Mendoza.
The crew reported flying at 10,000 feet and expected to reach Santiago at 17:30 UTC.
The crew again reported 10,000 feet. Their expected arrival time remained unchanged.
The crew received destination weather describing clouds and improving visibility at Los Cerrillos.
Near Mendoza, the crew reported climbing from 20,000 toward 24,000 feet and revised their arrival estimate.
The crew revised their expected arrival to 17:45 UTC. Their position and altitude are unknown.
The final message confirmed the expected arrival time and ended with a radio word.
The Santiago operator requested clarification. The aircraft repeated the word twice; the exact times aren't known.
The aircraft struck Tupungato in cloud, killing all eleven aboard. The exact time isn't known.
Los Cerrillos broadcast an announcement that the aircraft was missing.
Air traffic control presumed the aircraft had crashed because its estimated fuel supply would have run out.
The airline notified the British ministry by telephone in London the next day.
Searches began as weather improved. Argentine and Chilean aircraft and ground patrols found no confirmed trace.
Three Chilean military aircraft joined the search on August 5.
A U.S. aircraft searched Tupungato and nearby mountains on August 7, finding no confirmed wreckage.
A British mission was sent on August 18 and searched San Juan and Mendoza.
The British mission suspended its search on August 21. The aircraft remained missing.
An investigator visited the region on August 31. The wreckage had still not been found.
Without wreckage, the first inquiry could not establish a cause. Severe ice buildup remained a possibility.
Two mountaineers found aircraft remains on Tupungato in 1998.
Searchers returned in January 2000 and found wreckage and material identifying the aircraft.
Two Argentine Air Force helicopters landed and photographed the wreckage in February 2000.
A military patrol and an investigator reached the wreckage. The exact date is uncertain.
Damage suggested one engine was turning at impact and the main wheels were retracted.
Glacier ice carried the wreckage downhill. An avalanche may have buried it after impact.
Investigators concluded that an incorrect speed calculation and bad mountain weather contributed to the aircraft descending too soon.
DNA comparisons were reported in 2002. The final number of people identified remains unknown.
The final radio word remains unexplained despite later claims.

one_line: Star Dust struck Tupungato in cloud; glacier ice concealed the wreckage for decades.
status_why: Wreckage established a mountain collision after a navigation error; the precise descent and final radio word remain unexplained.
